title: Sultanate of Bima
capsule: The Sultanate of Bima emerged in eastern Sumbawa, Indonesia, when the Makassarese-backed prince La Kai accepted Islam in February 1621 and was installed as Sultan Abdul Kahir, the first sultan, converting a pre-existing Hindu-Buddhist kingdom into an Islamic polity. Bima traded horses, timber, and slaves and maintained close dynastic ties with the Makassarese nobility of Gowa; after the VOC defeated Gowa in 1667, the sultanate fell under Dutch suzerainty. The catastrophic 1815 eruption of Tambora — the most powerful volcanic event in recorded history — devastated the region, killing tens of thousands. Dutch control was formalized in a new contract in 1905 curtailing the sultan's foreign trade rights, and following Indonesian independence the sultanate was abolished in 1958 when the Indonesian republic replaced the Sumbawan principalities with modern administrative districts.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The sultanate's core territory in eastern Sumbawa is reasonably well-defined; Dutch colonial records document formal boundaries from the late 19th century, but earlier limits are approximate.
